newsitem.title: NORWAY: New Norway cabinet faces budget battle.
newsitem.headline: New Norway cabinet faces budget battle.

text.p: Thorbjoern Jagland became Norway's new prime minister on Friday, succeeding political veteran Gro Harlem Brundtland less than a year before the minority Labour government faces general elections.

But Jagland's first test of strength will be to shepherd the 1997 state budget through a hostile parliament. He said at his first news conference as premier that changes to the draft would have to be made in order for it to be accepted.
The government is under pressure from the opposition right and left of centre to use the country's massive oil wealth to increase expenditure before the budget is adopted in December.
King Harald V appointed Jagland, 46, and his new cabinet at a special session of the Council of State in the Royal Palace after accepting Brundtland's resignation.
"We must realise that there will be changes to the budget, but we don't want to change the balance we have struck," Jagland told reporters.
"But clearly we can change some priorities, and it is possible to increase spending on some areas and still maintain the balance we have," he said.
Jagland reaffirmed his government would continue the economic policies of Brundtland, 57, who has dominated Norwegian politics for 15 years and was in office for 10 of them.
"The pillar of the social welfare policy of this government is to keep on maintaining low price growth so that we can continue fighting unemployment," Jagland said.
In a surprise announcement on Wednesday Brundtland said she was stepping down to give Labour a fresh start for the general election next September.

Jagland as party leader has been groomed for years to become premier. Although economic and other policies will remain unchanged, he has put his stamp firmly on the new 18-member cabinet. It contains seven new names and four of the members retained from Brundtland's government are shifting portfolios.

Industry and Energy Minister Jens Stoltenberg is succeeding Sigbjoern Johnsen as finance minister. Johnsen, who has been criticised by the opposition and industry over a number of issues, becomes an ordinary member of parliament.
Stoltenberg will hand over his portfolio to Justice Minister Grete Faremo, who has emerged as a tough defender of Norway's strict immigration policies.
Faremo is replaced as justice minister by Anne Holt, one of Norway's most popular writers of detective stories.
Bjoern Tore Godal and Joergen Kosmo remain as foreign minister and defence minister respectively.
Special U.N. envoy Terje Roed Larsen, Norway's troubleshooter in the Middle East peace process, is moving back to Oslo from Israel to head a newly created ministry for national planning.

Stoltenberg, whose boyish charm and management of the country's oil wealth has earned him widespread popularity in opinion polls, will now manage a state budget projected to show a surplus of 40.9 billion crowns ($6.35 billion) in 1997.
Despite the huge surplus projected for next year, the government has said it will keep a tight grip on expenditure for fear of fuelling inflation.
A majority in parliament wants to raise spending in the 1997 budget partly through higher welfare payments and tax revisions.

Central bank governor Kjell Storvik said earlier this week any weakening of the 1997 state budget would be detrimental to a balanced economic development. He has urged parliament not to dilute the budget because there was a clear risk of further pressure on the economy and higher cost growth next year.
